lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing the Right Location and Stall Setup
lessons.body: Location is the single most important decision you will make as a small shop or market trader. A good location can double your daily sales while a poor one will slowly drain your capital through rent, transport and wasted hours. In most African markets, the best spots are near entrances, near transport stages, near busy footpaths, near schools, near places of worship, and near complementary businesses such as barbershops, phone charging points and food stalls. Before you commit to any space, spend at least three days watching the traffic. Count how many people pass between 6am and 9am, between noon and 2pm, and between 5pm and 8pm. Note what they are carrying, what they are wearing and whether they stop to buy from existing traders. Talk to neighbouring traders and ask them honestly how sales have been over the last month. If three or more traders tell you business is slow, believe them. Rent should never exceed ten to fifteen percent of your expected monthly gross sales. If a landlord demands more, walk away and keep searching. In many cities you can also negotiate with the local market association or council for a temporary space before committing to a long lease. Once you have your location, set up your stall or shop to make buying easy. Use vertical space with shelves, hooks and hanging displays. Keep the most profitable and fast-moving items at eye level. Put cheap impulse items such as sweets, airtime, matches and sachet water near the front where people brush past. Keep a clear walking path so customers do not feel trapped. Use bright colours on your signage but keep the words short and readable from five metres away. If you sell food, invest in a clean display case or at least a mesh cover to keep flies off. If you sell clothes, hang samples outside and keep stock inside in labelled bags. Lighting matters more than many traders realise. A simple solar bulb or rechargeable lamp allows you to trade for two extra hours in the evening when workers are returning home with money in their pockets. Security is also part of setup. Build a relationship with nearby traders so you can watch each other's goods. If you must leave stock overnight, use a strong lock, a metal box and, where possible, a shared storage arrangement with two or three trusted neighbours. Never keep all your cash in one pocket. Use a small bag tied inside your clothing and move excess money to a safe place or mobile money account during the day. Finally, keep your space clean. Sweep every morning and evening. Remove rubbish immediately. Customers in every African market judge a business by how it looks. A clean stall signals that you care about quality and that your goods are safe. A dirty stall signals the opposite, no matter how good your prices are. Treat your location and setup as a long-term investment, not a temporary arrangement, and you will build a customer base that returns week after week.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Stock Selection, Pricing and Profit Margins
lessons.body: Your profit lives or dies on what you buy and how you price it. Many small traders fail not because they lack customers but because they stock the wrong items, buy too little of what sells and too much of what does not, and price without knowing their true costs. Start by tracking your sales for two weeks. Write down every item you sell, the quantity and the price. At the end of each day, identify your top five sellers and your bottom five. The top five should get more space, more capital and more attention. The bottom five should be reduced or dropped unless they bring customers who also buy other things. When you buy stock, always calculate your landed cost. Landed cost includes the buying price, transport, market fees, packaging, any breakages and the cost of your time if you travel far. If you buy a carton of soap for 20,000 shillings and spend 2,000 on transport, your landed cost is 22,000. If the carton contains 48 bars, each bar costs about 458 shillings. If you sell each bar for 600, your gross profit is 142 shillings per bar, which is about 31 percent. That is a healthy margin for fast-moving goods. For slow-moving goods you need higher margins, often 50 percent or more, because your money is tied up longer. Never price by copying the next trader without checking your own numbers. They may buy in larger volumes, get credit from suppliers or sell at a loss to attract customers for other items. You need to know your break-even point. Add up your monthly rent, transport, airtime, packaging, security and any loan repayment. Divide that by your average gross profit per sale. The result is the number of sales you must make each month just to survive. Everything above that is real profit. Use this number to set daily targets and to decide whether a new product is worth stocking. When buying, negotiate hard but fairly. Build relationships with two or three reliable suppliers rather than chasing the cheapest price every week. A supplier who gives you consistent quality and small credit terms is worth more than one who saves you five percent but delivers late. Where possible, buy in groups with other traders to access wholesale prices. Many African markets have savings groups, table banking or chama arrangements that can fund bulk purchases. Keep your stock organised by category and rotate older stock to the front. Use the first in, first out rule, especially for food, cosmetics and medicine. Check expiry dates every week and remove anything close to expiry before customers find it. Damaged or expired stock destroys trust faster than high prices. Reinvest a fixed percentage of your profit, for example thirty percent, back into your best-selling lines. Use another percentage to test one new product each month. Test small, measure results and only scale up what works. Keep a simple notebook or phone app to record purchases, sales and expenses daily. At the end of each week, calculate your gross profit, your expenses and your net profit. If your net profit is falling, look first at your stock mix, then at your prices, then at your costs. Do not blame the economy until you have checked your own numbers. Discipline in stock selection and pricing is what separates traders who grow from traders who merely survive.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Customer Service, Trust and Repeat Business
lessons.body: In small shop and market trading, your reputation is your most valuable asset. A customer who trusts you will return, bring friends and forgive small mistakes. A customer who feels cheated will tell ten people and never come back. Customer service in African markets is not about fancy language or expensive uniforms. It is about respect, consistency, honesty and speed. Greet every customer, even the ones who are only looking. A simple good morning, welcome or how are you costs nothing and opens the door to a sale. Learn names where you can. If a customer buys from you three times, call them by name the fourth time. That single act creates loyalty stronger than any discount. Be honest about your products. If a phone battery is weak, say so. If a dress runs small, say so. If you do not have an item, tell the customer where they can find it rather than selling them something inferior. Short-term tricks destroy long-term income. If you make a mistake, such as giving wrong change or selling a faulty item, fix it immediately and without argument. Replace the item, refund the money or offer a fair alternative. Customers remember how you handled a problem far more than the problem itself. Speed matters. In busy markets, customers will walk away if they wait too long. Keep your stall arranged so you can find items quickly. Learn your prices by heart. Have small change ready in a separate pocket or tin. If you are serving several people, acknowledge everyone and tell them you will be with them shortly. Never ignore a customer while chatting with a friend or scrolling on your phone. That behaviour tells the customer their money is not important to you. Offer small extras that cost little but mean a lot. A plastic bag, a free matchbox, a sweet for a child or a quick phone charge can turn a one-time buyer into a regular. If you sell food, keep it hot, clean and well presented. If you sell clothes, allow trying on where possible and offer honest advice on fit and colour. If you sell airtime or mobile money, be fast and accurate, because trust in money services is fragile. Handle complaints calmly. Listen fully before responding. Do not raise your voice, even if the customer is wrong. If you cannot solve the problem on the spot, agree on a time when you will follow up and then do it. Keep a small notebook to record customer requests for items you do not stock. When you finally stock that item, call or message the customer. This simple habit builds a loyal following and reduces the risk of buying stock nobody wants. Build a customer community through WhatsApp groups or SMS lists where you announce new stock, price offers and market days. Do not spam. Send useful messages two or three times a week at most. Reward loyal customers with a small discount on their fifth purchase or a free item after a certain spend. Keep records of who buys what so you can personalise your service. Finally, protect your reputation online and offline. Ask satisfied customers to recommend you. If someone posts a complaint on social media, respond politely and offer to resolve it. In the market, never gossip about other traders or customers. What you say about others reveals your own character. Consistent, respectful, honest service is the cheapest and most powerful marketing available to any small trader in Africa.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Managing Money, Records and Mobile Payments
lessons.body: Money management is where most small traders lose the gains they make in sales. Cash flows in and out quickly, and without a system it is easy to spend stock money on personal needs, forget debts and miss opportunities. The first rule is to separate business money from personal money. Use a different pocket, bag or mobile money wallet for the business. If you can, open a separate bank or mobile money account for the shop. Even a simple wallet on your phone with a clear label helps. Pay yourself a fixed small salary each week rather than dipping into the till whenever you need something. The second rule is to record every transaction. You do not need expensive software. A notebook with columns for date, item, quantity, buying price, selling price and expenses is enough. At the end of each day, total your sales, total your expenses and calculate your cash position. At the end of each week, calculate your gross profit and net profit. At the end of each month, compare your results with the previous month. If you cannot explain where your money went, you cannot grow. The third rule is to manage credit carefully. Selling on credit is common in African markets and can build loyalty, but it can also destroy your business. Set clear rules. Only give credit to customers you know well. Write down the name, amount, date and agreed repayment date. Set a maximum credit limit, for example no more than ten percent of your daily sales. Follow up politely but firmly on the agreed date. If a customer fails to pay twice, stop giving credit until the old balance is cleared. Never lend stock money to friends or family without a written agreement and a repayment plan. The fourth rule is to use mobile money wisely. Mobile money has transformed trading across Africa, allowing fast payments, safe storage and remote transfers. Use it to pay suppliers, receive customer payments and save small amounts daily. But watch the transaction fees. If you receive many small payments, the charges can eat your margin. Encourage customers to buy slightly more to reduce the number of transactions, or absorb the fee into your price where the market allows. Keep your PIN secret. Never share your phone or wallet with anyone. Register your SIM in your own name and keep your ID safe. The fifth rule is to build a reserve. Aim to save at least five percent of your weekly sales in a separate wallet or savings group. This reserve covers emergencies such as stock damage, sickness, theft or a sudden price increase from suppliers. It also allows you to grab bargains when a wholesaler offers a discount for cash. The sixth rule is to plan for taxes and fees. Many traders ignore market fees, licences and local levies until they are confronted. Find out what you legally owe and budget for it weekly. Paying on time avoids fines and harassment and gives you peace of mind. Finally, review your numbers monthly with a clear head. Ask yourself which products made the most profit, which customers paid late, which expenses were unnecessary and what you will do differently next month. Share your numbers with a trusted mentor or savings group if it helps you stay accountable. Money discipline is not about being stingy. It is about respecting your own work enough to protect and grow it. Traders who keep clean records and control their cash consistently outperform those who rely on memory and luck.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Growth, Risk and Adapting to Change
lessons.body: Every small shop and market trader faces change. Prices rise, customers move, new competitors appear, technology shifts and seasons change. The traders who survive and grow are the ones who plan for risk and adapt quickly. Start by identifying your main risks. These usually fall into five groups: money risks such as theft, unpaid credit and sudden price increases; stock risks such as spoilage, damage and expiry; market risks such as new competitors, road closures or market relocation; personal risks such as sickness, family emergencies and burnout; and external risks such as floods, fires, currency changes and new regulations. Write down your top five risks and one practical action for each. For theft, for example, your action might be to bank or mobile-money your cash twice a day. For spoilage, it might be to buy smaller quantities of perishable goods and use a cooler or shade. For new competitors, it might be to focus on a niche such as fresh produce, phone accessories or tailoring that they do not serve well. Growth does not always mean a bigger stall. It can mean higher margins, more loyal customers, a second location, a delivery service or an online presence. Before you expand, strengthen your current business. Make sure your records are clean, your stock turns over well and your customer base is stable. Then test growth in small steps. If you want to add a new product line, buy a small quantity, display it well and track sales for one month. If it works, increase slowly. If it does not, cut your losses quickly. If you want a second stall, train a trusted family member or employee and put clear rules in place for cash, stock and pricing. Many African traders grow through partnerships, savings groups and cooperatives. Joining a strong group can give you access to bulk buying, credit, training and a network of customers. Choose your partners carefully. Look for people with a track record of honesty, hard work and clear communication. Put agreements in writing, even if it feels awkward. Adapt to technology. Mobile money, WhatsApp catalogues, Facebook Marketplace, Instagram and simple delivery apps are now part of trading in most African cities and towns. You do not need to be an expert. Start with one channel, such as a WhatsApp group for your regular customers. Post clear photos, prices and location. Respond quickly. Offer delivery for a small fee or free delivery above a certain order value. Keep your phone charged and your data bundle topped up. Adapt to seasons. In many regions, sales rise during harvest, school opening, festive periods and salary weeks, and fall during planting, exams and dry spells. Plan your stock and cash flow around these cycles. Build a buffer during peak months to carry you through slow months. Adapt to customer needs. If customers ask for smaller packs, offer them. If they ask for credit, set clear rules. If they ask for delivery, find a way to provide it. Finally, take care of yourself. Long hours, heavy loads, heat, dust and stress damage your health and judgement. Drink water, rest when you can, and seek medical help early. A healthy trader makes better decisions. Keep learning. Attend market association meetings, listen to business programmes on radio, watch short videos on your phone and talk to traders in other markets. Ask what is working for them and what is not. Set simple goals for the next three months, six months and one year. Review them monthly. Celebrate small wins and correct small mistakes before they become big ones. Growth is not a single leap. It is a series of small, disciplined, well-timed steps. With clear risk planning, honest records, strong customer relationships and a willingness to adapt, any small shop or market trader in Africa can build a business that supports a family, creates jobs and stands strong through change.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Daily Operating Standards for Small Shops and Market Traders

This Practical Reference lesson supports Module 5: Growth, Risk and Adapting to Change. It gives you a single place to check the numbers, routines and safety rules that keep a small shop or market stall profitable in African markets. Use it as a counter-top reference, a training sheet for helpers, and a checklist before you open and close each day.

The core business idea is simple: your margin is small, so your profit comes from volume, speed and low losses. A trader who sells 100 units at a 12% margin earns more than one who sells 40 units at a 20% margin. Daily standards protect that volume by keeping stock fresh, prices clear, cash accounted for, and customers returning.

Table 1: Typical Gross Margin Ranges by Product Category (African small shop / market context)

Product category Typical gross margin (%) Stock turnover (days) Main loss risk Practical action
Staples (maize flour, rice, sugar) 5â12% 7â14 Moisture, rodents Buy in bulk only if dry storage is secure
Cooking oil, salt, spices 10â18% 14â30 Leakage, expiry Rotate stock; keep sealed
Fresh vegetables & fruit 25â40% 1â3 Spoilage Buy small daily; sell before evening
Processed snacks & drinks 15â25% 7â21 Expiry, breakage Check dates weekly; front-face old stock
Airtime & mobile money float 2â5% commission Same day Float shortage Keep separate float; reconcile daily
Soap, detergent, toiletries 12â22% 14â30 Pilferage Keep behind counter; count weekly

Source: Ranges compiled from FAO agricultural market and retail trade guidance, and from university extension retail management bulletins for small-scale traders. Actual margins vary by country, season and supplier. Use these as a starting benchmark, then record your own real numbers for four weeks.

Table 2: Daily Cash Reconciliation Template (example figures in local currency units)

Item Example (Day 1) Example (Day 2) What it tells you
Opening cash float 20,000 23,500 Cash available to give change
Opening mobile money balance 15,000 18,200 Float for customer withdrawals
Cash sales 31,000 27,800 Main revenue stream
Mobile money sales 12,500 14,000 Growing digital revenue
Stock purchases (cash) 18,000 15,000 Cost of goods
Expenses (transport, airtime, rent) 4,500 3,800 Operating costs
Expected closing cash 28,500 32,500 Opening + cash sales â cash purchases â expenses
Actual closing cash 27,900 32,500 Counted at close
Difference â600 0 Investigate same day; do not ignore

Source: Template structure based on FAO and university extension small business record-keeping guidance. Example figures are illustrative only; replace with your own daily numbers.

â  SAFETY WARNING â FOOD, CHEMICALS AND HEALTH

If you sell food, drinks, or any chemical product (pesticides, bleach, rat poison, fuel), you must separate them completely. Never store chemicals near food, drinks, cooking oil, or animal feed. Never repackage pesticides or chemicals into drink bottles, cooking oil containers, or food bags â this causes fatal poisoning, especially for children. Wash hands with soap after handling money, raw meat, or chemicals. Keep raw meat, poultry and eggs away from cooked food and ready-to-eat items. If a customer reports illness after buying food from you, stop selling that batch immediately, keep a sample if possible, and contact your local public health officer. For chemical poisoning, contact a poison control centre or the nearest health facility immediately â do not wait.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Opening: Count cash and mobile money float; write the opening balance before the first sale.
  • Stock: Check fast-moving items; remove expired, damaged or spoiled goods from the selling area.
  • Prices: Display clear prices for at least your top 10 products; update when supplier prices change.
  • Sales record: Record every sale, including small credit sales, in a notebook or phone app the same day.
  • Mobile money: Confirm each transaction with the SMS or app receipt before releasing goods or cash.
  • Expenses: Keep receipts for transport, rent, airtime and any other business cost.
  • Closing: Count cash, check mobile money balance, and compare with expected closing balance.
  • Difference: If cash is short or over, investigate the same day and write down the reason.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale food retail and market hygiene guidance
  • ILRI â Publications on livestock and market value chains in Africa
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food manual
  • MSD Animal Health â Animal health and food safety resources
  • Penn State Extension â Business and money management for small enterprises

Use this reference page at your stall every day. The traders who grow are not the ones with the biggest capital â they are the ones who count, record, and correct the small differences before they become big losses.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of keeping a daily sales record in a small shop?
options: A) To impress customers with neat handwriting
B) To track income, expenses, and stock movement
C) To replace the need for a bank account
D) To avoid paying taxes legally
quiz.explanation: A daily sales record helps a trader monitor money coming in, money going out, and how fast stock is moving.

quiz.q: Which pricing method adds a fixed amount to the cost price of each item?
options: A) Loss leader pricing
B) Penetration pricing
C) Cost plus markup pricing
D) Psychological pricing
quiz.explanation: Cost plus markup pricing sets the selling price by adding a fixed profit amount or percentage to the cost price.

quiz.q: Why is it important to separate business money from personal money in a small shop?
options: A) It makes the shop look more professional
B) It is required only for large supermarkets
C) It helps customers pay faster
D) It gives a clear picture of true business profit or loss
quiz.explanation: Mixing personal and business money hides the real performance of the shop and makes profit calculation unreliable.

quiz.q: What does stock turnover measure in market trading?
options: A) How quickly goods are sold and replaced
B) How many customers visit the stall daily
C) How much rent is paid for the stall
D) How many suppliers a trader has
quiz.explanation: Stock turnover shows how fast inventory moves from the shop or stall to customers and is replaced.

quiz.q: Which action best helps a market trader reduce the risk of running out of popular items?
options: A) Buying only luxury goods
B) Monitoring sales trends and reordering early
C) Raising prices every week
D) Keeping all money in a personal wallet
quiz.explanation: Watching which items sell fastest and reordering before stock runs low prevents lost sales.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to calculate gross profit for a small shop?
options: A) Total sales minus rent only
B) Total sales minus cost of goods sold
C) Total expenses plus personal spending
D) Total stock value plus cash in hand
quiz.explanation: Gross profit is total sales revenue minus the cost of the goods that were sold.

quiz.q: Why should a trader record credit sales separately from cash sales?
options: A) Credit sales are always illegal
B) Cash sales do not affect profit
C) Credit sales represent money still owed to the business
D) Credit customers never return to buy again
quiz.explanation: Credit sales are not yet paid for, so they must be tracked as amounts owed to avoid cash flow problems.

quiz.q: Which practice helps protect a small shop from theft and stock loss?
options: A) Leaving the till open for quick access
B) Allowing anyone to take goods on trust
C) Counting stock only once a year
D) Doing regular stock counts and keeping records secure
quiz.explanation: Regular stock counts and secure records help detect missing items early and discourage theft.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when choosing a location for a small shop in an African market?
options: A) Proximity to a popular nightclub
B) Foot traffic and accessibility for customers
C) Being far from other shops to avoid competition
D) A location with no transport links
quiz.explanation: High foot traffic and easy access bring more potential customers to your shop.

quiz.q: What is a key consideration for stall setup in an open-air market?
options: A) Using expensive imported materials only
B) Making the stall as tall as possible
C) Clear display and protection from sun and rain
D) Hiding goods so thieves cannot see them
quiz.explanation: Good display attracts customers while protection keeps goods safe from weather.

quiz.q: Why is it important to arrange goods at eye level in a stall?
options: A) It makes the stall look empty
B) Customers are more likely to notice and buy
C) It reduces the weight of the goods
D) It prevents customers from touching items
quiz.explanation: Eye-level products are more visible and easier for customers to notice and buy.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a good location for a small trading business?
options: A) Near a busy bus stop or market entrance
B) On a quiet street with no pedestrians
C) Next to a police station only
D) In an area with no mobile network
quiz.explanation: Bus stops and market entrances have high pedestrian traffic, increasing sales opportunities.

quiz.q: When selecting stock for a small shop, what should you prioritise?
options: A) Items that are cheapest to buy regardless of demand
B) Products that customers frequently ask for
C) Only luxury items for wealthy customers
D) Items that expire very quickly
quiz.explanation: Stocking what customers want ensures faster sales and less dead stock.

quiz.q: What does profit margin mean?
options: A) The total amount of money in your till
B) The difference between selling price and cost price
C) The number of items sold in a day
D) The rent you pay for your stall
quiz.explanation: Profit margin is the amount left after subtracting the cost of the item from its selling price.

quiz.q: If you buy an item for 10 and sell it for 15, what is your profit?
quiz.explanation: Profit is selling price minus cost price, so 15 minus 10 equals 5.

quiz.q: Why should a trader avoid pricing goods too low?
options: A) It attracts too many customers
B) It may not cover costs and lead to losses
C) It makes the shop look expensive
D) It reduces the need for record keeping
quiz.explanation: Prices that are too low may not cover costs and can cause the business to lose money.

quiz.q: What is a good way to build trust with customers?
options: A) Selling expired goods at a discount
B) Being honest about product quality and prices
C) Changing prices every hour
D) Ignoring customer complaints
quiz.explanation: Honesty about quality and fair pricing builds trust and encourages repeat business.

quiz.q: Why is greeting customers important in African market settings?
options: A) It wastes time and slows sales
B) It creates a friendly atmosphere and encourages buying
C) It is required by law
D) It scares away competitors
quiz.explanation: A warm greeting makes customers feel welcome and more likely to return.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer complains about a product?
options: A) Argue with them loudly
B) Listen calmly and try to resolve the issue
C) Tell them to leave and never return
D) Blame the supplier and do nothing
quiz.explanation: Listening and resolving complaints shows you value customers and helps retain them.

quiz.q: How can a trader encourage repeat business?
options: A) Offering small loyalty rewards or discounts
B) Raising prices every week
C) Selling only to new customers
D) Closing the shop at random times
quiz.explanation: Loyalty rewards and discounts give customers a reason to come back.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep business money separate from personal money?
options: A) It makes it harder to know your profit
B) It helps you track business performance accurately
C) It is illegal to mix them
D) It reduces the amount of cash you have
quiz.explanation: Separating money helps you see whether the business is making a profit or loss.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to keep daily sales records?
options: A) Memorising all sales
B) Writing sales in a notebook or using a mobile app
C) Asking customers to remember for you
D) Only recording sales on weekends
quiz.explanation: A notebook or mobile app provides a simple and reliable record of daily sales.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of accepting mobile money payments?
options: A) It increases the risk of theft
B) It offers convenience and attracts more customers
C) It requires no record keeping
D) It is only for large businesses
quiz.explanation: Mobile money is convenient, safer than carrying cash, and attracts customers who prefer digital payments.

quiz.q: What should you do before accepting a mobile payment?
options: A) Confirm the payment has been received in your account
B) Assume the customer has paid
C) Give goods before checking
D) Ask the customer to pay later
quiz.explanation: Always confirm the payment is received before releasing goods to avoid losses.

quiz.q: What is a key risk for small traders in African markets?
options: A) Too many customers
B) Theft and loss of stock
C) Having too much profit
D) Selling out too quickly
quiz.explanation: Theft and stock loss are common risks that can seriously affect a small business.

quiz.q: How can a trader adapt to changing customer demand?
options: A) Keep selling the same products forever
B) Observe trends and adjust stock accordingly
C) Ignore customer feedback
D) Close the business
quiz.explanation: Observing trends and adjusting stock helps a trader stay relevant and profitable.

quiz.q: What is a good way to grow a small trading business?
options: A) Reinvesting some profits into more stock
B) Spending all profits on personal items
C) Borrowing money without a plan
D) Reducing stock variety
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting profits allows the business to buy more stock and grow gradually.

quiz.q: Why is it important to have a small emergency fund for your business?
options: A) To pay for unexpected costs like repairs or stock replacement
B) To lend to friends and family
C) To buy luxury items
D) To avoid paying taxes
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund helps the business survive unexpected expenses without collapsing.

quiz.q: What does the practical reference suggest about pricing?
options: A) Set prices randomly
B) Consider cost, competition and customer demand
C) Always charge the lowest price
D) Never change prices
quiz.explanation: Good pricing considers cost, what competitors charge, and what customers are willing to pay.

quiz.q: Which practice helps a trader manage risk effectively?
options: A) Keeping all cash at the stall overnight
B) Diversifying products and keeping records
C) Ignoring market changes
D) Lending stock to everyone
quiz.explanation: Diversifying products and keeping good records reduces risk and helps the business adapt.
